title: What is a linked list: a chain of nodes, each node holds data + a pointer to the next node; unlike array, nodes are NOT stored side by side in memory.
keyPoints: A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds data and a next reference to the following node
The list is accessed through a head reference; the last node's next points to null
Nodes are scattered on the heap and connected only by references, not stored contiguously like an array
Inserting or deleting at the head is O(1) because you only re-point a reference, while array insertion shifts elements
Random access is O(n) because you must walk from the head, unlike O(1) index-based array access
A doubly linked list adds a previous pointer so you can traverse in both directions
Linked lists have poor cache locality compared to arrays, so iteration is slower in practice despite the same big-O

s1_definition.oneliner: A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next node, connected by references rather than by sitting side by side in memory.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Node** – the building block; each node stores a piece of data and a `next` reference pointing to the following node in the chain.
- **Head** – a reference to the first node in the list; this is the only entry point for traversal.
- **Tail** – the last node whose `next` reference is `null`, signaling the end of the chain.
- **Non-contiguous storage** – unlike an array, nodes live anywhere on the heap and are connected only by their `next` pointers.
- **Singly vs doubly** – a singly linked list has only a `next` pointer; a doubly linked list adds a `prev` pointer for backward traversal.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a chain of pending loan applications for Rajesh. Each application slip has the loan details plus an arrow pointing to the next slip. The slips are scattered in different drawers across the office, but each one tells the clerk exactly where the next one is. The clerk starts from the first slip (the head) and follows arrows until a slip's arrow points to nothing, which marks the end of the pending queue.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A linked list is one of the most fundamental data structures in computer science. It is a chain of nodes where each node holds a piece of data and a reference to the next node. Unlike an array, the nodes are not stored side by side in memory. They can live anywhere on the heap, and the only thing connecting them is the `next` pointer inside each node. You access the list through a `head` reference that points to the first node, and you reach any other node by walking the chain one step at a time.

The key trade-off between a linked list and an array is access versus modification. An array gives you O(1) random access by index because elements sit in a contiguous block, but inserting at the front costs O(n) because every element must shift. A linked list gives you O(1) insertion and deletion at the head because you only re-point a reference, but reaching the fifth node means walking through the first four, so access is O(n). A doubly linked list adds a `prev` pointer so you can traverse backwards, which is how Java's `java.util.LinkedList` is implemented internally.

In practice, linked lists have poor cache locality because the nodes are scattered across memory, so for pure sequential iteration an `ArrayList` is faster even though the big-O is the same. The real value of understanding linked lists lies in coding interviews, where reversal, cycle detection, merging, and fast-slow pointer problems are staples, and in understanding the internals of structures like `LinkedHashMap` and `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, we use a linked list to model Rajesh's pending loan application queue. New applications arrive at the front in constant time, and processed applications are removed from the front in constant time. We rarely need random access into the middle of the queue, so the linked list is a natural fit.

Remember one sentence: a linked list is a chain of heap-scattered nodes connected by `next` pointers, trading O(1) random access for O(1) head insertion.
